title.official: Time limitation on reviewing retainer agreements and charges

division.heading: Lawyers’ Charges, Retainer Agreements and Right of Review

operative_text.controlling:
10.10(1)  A retainer agreement may not be reviewed if 6 months
has passed after the date on which the retainer agreement
terminated.
(2)  A lawyer’s charges may not be reviewed, whether at the
request of the lawyer or the client, if one year has passed after the
date on which the account was sent to the client.

BOOK_A.title: Time Limitation on Reviewing Retainer Agreements and Charges
BOOK_A.commentary:
Subrule 2 was amended in 2020 to extend the time limit from 6 months to one year.
This Rule sets ordinary time limits⁶
for a client (or other person liable to pay) seeking to review
the lawyer’s account which he or she owes. The time limits probably do not apply to interim

accounts, but what is an interim account is a matter of some debate in the many recent cases.¹
One would not think that how to compute the time for review was otherwise difﬁcult, but it can be.²
The court can extend the time limit, and case law gives 4 or 6 factors to consider then.³
When
can the court extend time?⁴
Speciﬁcally on this topic, sympathy for the client often unduly intrudes.⁵
Prejudice,⁶
whether the statement of account was interim or ﬁnal,⁷
and evidence of overcharging,
are important. Various fact situations come up in the cases.⁸
The threshold for extending time is
not low, and neither the client's good-faith desires nor some evidence of overcharging or that the
account should be reviewed, sufﬁces. The time limit balances both sides' interests. The time limit
is mandatory law, not mere advice.⁹

Extending time without notice is questionable.¹
The time limit applies only to review at the instance of the client, as otherwise a lawyer could
be time-barred without knowing that there is an issue.²
The time limit for review did not bar review
here because (at the clients' request) some of the services were rendered well after the invoice
for them! And R.10.24 is separate and more speciﬁc than R.10.10(2).³
The modern rules of interpretation of statutes apply also to the Rules of Court, and that
includes (though with less weight) their statement of their purpose, so long as speciﬁc operational
words are not distorted. Rules 1.2 and 1.7 were looked at, and applied to R.10.10 (time limit for
review of a legal account).⁴
What is subject to the deadline (a year plus 75 days if in 2020),⁵
despite some conﬂict in
authority, is to be interpreted purposively, contextually, and harmoniously with other Rules,
including R.10.13(4). So this deadline stops running when the Appointment is obtained, even if
it has not yet been served. Service within a reasonable time sufﬁces. If there is undue delay in
serving, that can be managed by the Review Ofﬁcer, who has many applicable powers.⁶
Like most time limits, breach of these ones must be somehow raised in a reasonable time, not
held silently until a late stage in the proceedings.⁷
Some objections to a lawyer’s account would be within the jurisdiction of a review ofﬁcer,
some for only a judge. If both kinds are present, an Applications Judge can order that the review
proceed ﬁrst (before a review ofﬁcer).⁸
See further on which topics a review ofﬁcer can and cannot
decide, notes to Rr.10.17 and 10.18.
This is a limitation period, even though in some circumstances it can be extended. So the
mandatory Ministerial Order made by the Minister of Justice applies and is mandatory. Because
of almost inaccessible courthouses, it extends time to commence proceedings by 75 days, from
March 17, 2020 to June 1, 2020, and those 75 days cannot be counted in calculating the time limit
for commencing (suing), and under this Rule the 75 days were not counted.⁹

footnotes.text: Does the court have inherent power outside this Rule? Avramenko v. Laurich, infra. The Limitations Act also applies: Samson Cree N. v. O’Reilly, infra. The two-year limitation period under that Act does not start to run from an interim provisional bill, only from a ﬁnal one: Brownlee v. Piccin Bottos 2014 ABCA 377, Calg 1401 0116 AC (Nov 18) ; Eryn B Logie Family Tr. v. West 2017 ABQB 339, 59 Alta LR(6th) 204 (¶ 20). And if the contract between lawyer and client gives 30 days to pay each account, the time (limitation period) does not begin to run until the 30 days ends: Pellerin Savitz LLP v. Guindon 2017 SCC 29, [2017] 1 SCR 575.

See the C. P. E. , Chapter 82, Part T.2; Samson Cree N. (Yellowbird) v. O’Reilly & Assoc.2013 ABQB 350, 564 AR 169, affd 2014 ABCA 268, 375 DLR(4th) 663; Re Van Brabant Est.2013 ABQB 547, JCE ES03 132119 (Sep 19) ; Eryn B Logie etc. v. West, supra. That the billing is to be based entirely on time, not on success or failure, is an important factor: Logie v. West. In Quebec, a contract for lawyer's work is not one for a ﬁnished product, but one of services for a certain period of time, so time to sue on an individual account can run and expire long before the end of the contract: Pellerin v. Guindon, supra. Would that apply outside Quebec? That ethics may bar the lawyer from suing his or her client for unpaid bills, while the lawyer still acts, does not suspend the statutory limitation period to sue from running: Pellerin v. Guindon.
See the C. P. E. Chapter 82, Part T.3.

See Poundmakers Lodge v. Scott & Co.2002 ABQB 745; Karl Mueller Constr. v. Miller Thomson (M 18 Dec ’02) JDE 0203 12114; Samson Cree N. v. O’Reilly, supra. The criteria are reviewed in Payne v. Evans Pearson & Co.2005 ABQB 12; Prophet R. F. N. v. Rath & Co.2011 ABQB 408, [2011] AR Uned 474. A fairly short time limit is reasonable where it is the client who wants to review the bill as the client knows from the beginning whether he has any concerns and it lets the law ﬁrm know where it stands: BA Cap. v. Focused Money Solutions (M) 2012 ABQB 379, [2012] AR Uned 386 (Jun 7). The factors were not satisﬁed in Samson Cree N. v. O’Reilly, supra. Notice of dissatisfaction was timely, and failure to explain the delay was not enough to bar review, in Thistle v. Stringham Denecky, infra; cf. Re Van Brabant Est. , supra. Grounds to doubt the size or computation of the accountant’s only became apparent late in the history, in Lewis Est. Communities v. Brownlee, infra. A vague description of the test, citing little authority, is found in Blake Cassels v. Baker Hughes Can. Co.2019 ABQB 233, JCC 1801 06490. Sed quaere.
Generally, on extending time, see R.12.5 and the C. P. E. , Chapter 18, Parts G to Q.

See a large number of examples in the C. P. E. , Chapter 82, Part T.5. A very lax test for extending time is suggested in Eryn B Logie etc. v. West, supra (¶’s 21-26) ; cf. Blake Cassels v. Baker Hughes Can. Co. , supra. Quaere; that is hard to reconcile with Samson Cree v. O'Reilly, supra. On taxing the account but only later reviewing the retainer, see Torode v. Smyth (#1) 2009 ABQB 601, 80 CPC(6th) 378. (And see (#2) 2009 ABQB 682. )

Some decisions on what is or is not prejudice seem rather counter-intuitive: Thistle v. Stringam Denecky 2013 ABQB 372, 567 AR 41; Lewis Est. Communities v. Brownlee 2013 ABQB 508, [2013] AR Uned 508; Re Van Brabant Est.2013 ABQB 547, 2013 CarswellAlta 1876.
See also Larocque v. Kantor LLP 2024 ABKB 327, JCC 2101 13183 (May 31).

Lappoehn v. Fleming Kambeitz (M) 2003 ABQB 497, 37 CPC(5th) 386 (late taxation of a series of accounts. The client could not have earlier long-paid accounts taxed, as alleged “new” evidence had been available earlier. The time for suing the lawyer had expired. But in another case, a lawyer’s bill was fully paid, out of trust. The 6 months expired. The contingency agreement was ambiguous. Some disbursements were unusual and not all may have been notiﬁed outside six months. Time to tax the bill was extended: Payne v. Evans Pearson & Co.2005 ABQB 12. Time to tax legal accounts was extended. Prejudice is a bar, but its absence is not enough. All were related bills in one retainer. Arguable case of overcharging, or insufﬁcient disclosure of retainer account: Berndt & Streitmeier v. Murdoch (M 10 Jun ’05) JDE 0403 05547. The contingency fee seemed miscalculated, so the Applications Judge allowed taxation? The application for taxation was within the 2-year limitation period. The other account could not be taxed. Neither was interim, and they were about different questions and opponents, albeit the same accident: Avramenko v. Laurich & Assoc. (M) 2006 ABQB 489, 405 AR 355. Here it took 16 months and there was no real explanation and certainly no sworn evidence on the subject. The court did not get to the next step of whether there was prejudice to the law ﬁrm. Time was not extended: BA Cap. v. Focused, supra.

West v. Logie Fam. Law 2018 ABCA 255, 72 Alta LR(6th) 52 (¶’s 20-26). Cases looking at whether the account in question is arguably too high, or suspicious, are illogical. That is a topic for a later stage, after time is extended. In no other area of the law is extending time based on an arguable case. Its absence may bar a time extension, but its presence only leads one to the usual factors to extend any time limit.
West v. Logie Fam. Law, supra (¶ 36).
Twinn v. Sawridge Band 2012 ABQB 44, 531 AR 158 (appending older unreported case law).
Lising v. Smith 2018 ABQB 1061, JCE 1803 13042. Quaere.
Rath & Co. v. Sturgeon L. Cree N. , infra (¶’s 30-38).
Spark Power Corp. v. Peacock Linder Hall 2022 ABKB 853, JCC 2001 10156 (Dec 16) (¶’s 12-16).

Spark Power v. Peacock, supra (¶’s 17-29) ; Rath & Co. v. Sturgeon L. Cree N.2022 ABQB 556, JCC 1801 11136 (Aug 18) (¶’s 39-59) ; Mikisew Cree F. N. v. Rath & Co.2023 ABKB 321, JCE 2203 02843 (May 30) (¶’s 48-50).
Moll v. MacPherson Leslie & Co.2014 ABCA 45, 569 AR 69.
O’Chiese F. N. v. DLA Piper (Can. ) 2022 ABCA 197, 49 Alta LR(7th) 280.

BOOK_B.title: Time limitation on reviewing retainer agreements and charges

commentary.text: Rule 10.10 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.10. 1. Time Limit Does Not Apply To Lawyers Seeking Review Please note that Twinn v. Sawridge Band, 2012 ABQB 44, 2012 CarswellAlta 104, was decided when the rule read: (2) A lawyer's charges may not be reviewed if 6 months has passed after the date on which the account was sent to the client. Subsequent to the decision in Twinn, in 2013 the wording of Rule 10.10(2) was changed to read (2) A lawyer's charges may not be reviewed, whether at the request of the lawyer or the client, if 6 months has passed after the date on which the account was sent to the client. The Alberta Court of Queen's Bench (Master Wacowich, in Chambers) considered the new wording in O'Brien v. de Villars Jones, 2015 ABQB 535, 2015 CarswellAlta 1546, stating as follows: 4 The Applicant then served an appointment for review on the client Ms. O'Brien on July 21, 2015. The Applicant submits that the 2013 accounts were proper as allowed in the case of Twinn v. Sawridge Band, 2012 ABQB 44, [2012] A.J. No. 59, 531 A.R. 158, 74 Alta. L.R. (5th) 371 (Alta. Q.B.). The Twinn case held that the then existing Rule 10.10(2) six month period applied only to client initiated reviews. 5 Rule 10.10(2) currently reads: A lawyer's charges may not be reviewed, whether at the request of the lawyer or the client, if 6 months has passed after the date on which the account was sent to the client. 6 The words “whether at the request of the lawyer or the client” were added to the rule on July 25, 2013, by amendment to the rule. These words were not present when the Twinn case was decided. 7 As indicated, the Review Officer was of the view that the amendment to the rule means that lawyers have to comply with the six month time limit. Unless one ignores the added wording lawyers are now bound by the six month term. … 21 Counsel for the Applicant indicates that the purpose of a lawyer initiated review has not changed since Browne J.'s decision in Twinn. She submits that new amended rule does not change Browne J.'s reasoning as to why the rule should not be changed. But the fact is that the Rule has clearly expressly made the rule applicable to lawyers. 22 I have been unable to find any notice to the profession or any report by the Alberta Law Reform Institute Report concerning this issue. However, it is clear that the rules require a six month limitation on the 2013 invoices of the Applicant. 23 As the rule has changed the law as set out in the Twinn case it is necessary for me to determine whether I should extend the six month time limit in Rule 10.10(2) to permit a review of the accounts of August 9, 2013 and December 24, 2013. 24 If I do not extend the time then the Applicant will be required to commence an action against its ex-client to enforce the money rightfully due to it. This will be using up the time of both lawyer and client and be an expense to both lawyer and client. While normally an extension considers using costs as a remedy for granting the extension I do not believe that is appropriate under these circumstances for all of the reasons set out by Browne, J. in Twinn. In my view it is poor policy to force a lawfirm to sue their client when there is another remedy easily available for the benefit of both lawyer and client. Accordingly, it is my view that unless the lawyer's account is so stale dated that it is statute barred by the Limitations Act I would grant the extension. 25 In the result it is my decision that the amended rule 10.10(2) prevents a review of a lawyer's charges if six months have passed after the date on which the account was sent to the client. Further, for the reasons cited, the Applicant law firm is granted an extension of the six months sufficient to allow for the taxation of the accounts of August 9, 2013 and December 24, 2013. It may therefore be the case that the decision in Twinn has been overtaken by legislative amendment and, while the decision in O'Brien cannot be said to have overruled Twinn, both decisions should be considered until such time as the Court of Appeal considers and clarifies the matter. 2. What must be done within the time period set out in the Rule? In Rath & Company Barristers & Solicitors v. Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation, 2022 ABQB 556, 2022 CarswellAlta 2136, Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation was a client of Rath & Company Barristers & Solicitors. The client wished to have reviewed an account it received from its lawyers. At the time, Rule 10.10(2) stated that “a lawyer's charges may not be reviewed … if 6 months has passed after the date on which the account was sent to the client.” The appointment for review obtained by the client, while obtained within 6 months of the date when the lawyer's account was sent to the client, set a review date beyond the 6 month period. Did the notice of appointment have to be filed and served within that 6 month period? Justice B.B. Johnston held that it did not, and said: [58] I find that when examined in their entire context, the express words of the rule support an interpretation than an appointment must be filed but not served, within the six month period articulated in rule 10.10. … [59] As I stated above, I agree with Master Prowse that statutory timelines are mandatory. However, in this case, the mandatory requirement in rule 10.10 relates to filing and not service. … Justice Kraus, in Spark Power Corp. v. Peacock Linder Halt & Mack LLP, 2022 ABKB 853, 2022 CarswellAlta 3644 at para. 23, agreed with Justice Johnston's comments in Rath & Company Barristers & Solicitors v. Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation, 2022 ABQB 556, 2022 CarswellAlta 2136. 3. Taxation Is Not Mandatory Rule 647 clearly implies taxation is not mandatory. Dennis W. Crowe Professional Corp. v. Allford (1983), 26 Alta. L.R. (2d) 21 (Q.B.), at 25, per Holmes J. In P., Barristers & Solicitors v. Legal Aid Society (Alberta) (1994), 26 Alta. L.R. (3d) 167 (Q.B.), Fruman J. noted that lawyers may sue for their fees or use the taxation rules. At p. 173, her Ladyship said: A solicitor is not required to proceed to taxation in order to collect an account from an unwilling client. The solicitor may proceed by way of statement of claim in the Court of Queen's Bench, or, if the monetary amount is within the jurisdiction of the Provincial Court, by way of a civil claim in that Court. Where the alternative is an action in the Court of Queen's Bench, a taxation may offer an expedited and less expensive collection procedure. After the account has been taxed and the appeals exhausted, the solicitor may seek an Order for Judgment and costs from the Master. The Judgment, if granted, permits the solicitor to file a writ and become an execution creditor. 4. Types of Retainers and Accounts In Samson Cree Nation v. O'Reilly & Associés, 2013 ABQB 350, 2013 CarswellAlta 1065, 564 A.R. 169, 46 C.P.C. (7th) 341, the client contested lawyer's accounts which had been rendered to it. In the course of deciding whether the review (taxation) of the accounts could proceed, A.C.J. Rooke set out a comprehensive review of the type of retainers and accounts which can exist. At the paragraph numbers noted below, his Lordship said: 18 Legal retainers and accounts have changed over the years6—indeed, over the last century and a half, and even more so in the last few decades. Some of the common law from older cases reflects the traditions of those times, and often, those common law principles have failed to reflect more modern practices. In the litigation field this is because litigation has changed from simple actions and short trials, to complex actions and long trials (sometimes a “mega trial”, as here). Parlee cited the following decisions: Sharma v. 643454 Alberta Ltd, 2006 ABQB 119, at para 39 (Slatter J, as he then was); Abedi v. Pennington, [2000] 2 Costs LR 205, 2000 WL 281290 (Engl CA), at p 205; and Davidsons v. Jones-Fenleigh, [1997] Costs LR 70, 1980 WL 149540 (Engl CA), at pp 2–3 to describe, accurately in my view, the old common law tradition: Historically, actions did not typically remain outstanding for lengthy periods of time, and were comparatively simple matters. At common law, lawyers were not permitted to terminate their retainer with their client until all of their work pursuant to that retainer was complete. In other words, they could not terminate their retainer until the trial judgment of the common law court was obtained. Nor could a lawyer at common law issue a final account until such time. Although they could and sometimes did issue some interim accounts, they were not permitted to enforce their accounts until the matter was complete and they had issued a final account. [Emphasis added] … 21 The consequences of characterizing a retainer as an entire agreement for taxation purposes was that, provided the client sought taxation within the limitation period pertaining to the final account, all interim and provisional accounts since the beginning of the retainer and the final account could be included in the taxation. Thus, when analysing those old cases and applying the appropriate law to more modern cases, it is important to understand this phenomenon. As we will see, old common law principles do not necessarily respond to current realities. This is particularly true in this case, because I have found that many of the arguments were incorrectly based on old and no longer applicable common law principles that are at odds with the terms of the retainer agreed by the parties. 22 As we will see, there have historically been a number of types of retainers and accounts based on common law assumptions. However, specific agreements (express or implied), often trumped such presumptions at common law. 23 It is now clear in Alberta that those historical common law principles, which previously set retainers, types of account, and taxation consequences, are no longer the law. The law has changed to reflect the modern realities of practice, and the terms of retainers, accounts, and their taxation consequences, must now be determined based on the particular facts of the particular retainer and accounts, rather than on antiquated general “rules”. To follow up (and put to rest) the policy arguments that say the requirement to tax lawyers accounts within a limitation period in a continuing retainer might be contrary to public policy by “straining, if not rupturing, the solicitor-client relationship before the retainer has ended”, there is an off-setting pubic policy provision that lawyers are not to be subject to surprise taxation after many years in a complex and lengthy case unless the retainer allows that. The result is to look at all the facts and circumstances around the case and determine what, in fact, was the agreement between the parties and then apply the effects of the law to it. B. — Current Legal Rights and Obligations Relating to Retainers and Accounts 1. — Types of Retainers and Accounts are Questions of Fact 24 In Sharma, at para 39, Slatter J, referencing a number of older cases, described the old common law and established the new practice: It is common practice for a lawyer to issue a series of interim accounts on a file, followed by a final account when the retainer is complete. The law has often treated the interim accounts as being provisional only, and not “final” until the final account is rendered: see Raithby v. Fraser & Beatty (2000), 47 O.R. (3d) 245 (Ont. S.C.J.) at para. 16; Enterprise Rent-a-Car Co. v. Shapiro, Cohen, Andrews, Findlayson (1998), 38 O.R. (3d) 257 (Ont. C.A.); Siegel v. Cameron & Cameron, [1996] A.J. No. 757 (Alta. Q.B.); Nathanson, Schachter & Thompson v. Levitt, 2004 BCSC 1402 (B.C.S.C.); Poundmakers Lodge v. Scott & Co., 2002 ABQB 745 (Alta. Q.B.), at para 19. Whether an interim account is final, or merely an advance billing must be decided in each case: Morin, Grant v. Olsson (1994), 37 C.P.C. (3d) 130 (B.C.S.C.[in Chambers]) at para. 130. [Emphasis and double emphasis added] … 27 Enterprise Rent-a-Car Co v. Shapiro, Cohen, Andrews, Finlayson (1998), 38 OR (3d) 257 (Ont CA) at para 13, is further authority that such matters are a question of fact, and that “some periodic bills can be final. A periodic bill can be final if it was the clear intention of both parties that the bill be final…”. [Emphasis added] To the same effect, see Feldstein & Associates Professional Corporation v. Kermidopulos, 2007 CanLii 40202 (Ont SC—Murray, J), at para 35, relying on Re Fellowes, McNeil v. Kansa Management Services Inc, (1997) 34 O.R. (3rd) 301 (ON CA). 2. — Types of Retainers, and Taxation Consequences 28 There were, and continue to be, a number of different types of retainers for legal services, and accounts rendered pursuant to those retainers. The nature of the retainer is closely tied to the type of account rendered. The parties' agreement as to the nature of the accounts to be rendered may be relevant to a finding of what the parties agreed to in the retainer, and conversely, the nature of the retainer may inform the nature of the accounts. a. — End of Cause/Whole (or Entire) Contract 29 There once was a time when pursuant to common law, and now only by contract, counsel was retained to take a matter to trial—or beyond—and no account was/would be delivered until the trial—at least—was over. At the conclusion one, and only one, account was delivered. This is often described as “a whole contract” or “an entire contract”: Abedi, at para. 1. … 31 The burden of proving that the periodic accounts of lawyers are final is upon the lawyers: Davis & Company v. Jiwan, 2006 BCSC 658, para. 73. 32 The Nation relies upon Avramenko v. Laurich & Associates, 2006 ABQB 489 (Master Hanebury), at para. 42 for the proposition (relying upon Enterprise) that to determine whether an account is final, the Court should consider: • whether the accounts relate to one matter or one piece of litigation, or part of a continuum. The accounts at Bar relate to one matter that is continuing as separate phases of litigation; • whether the accounts were marked “final”. The Nation argued that some accounts were marked “interim”, but I reviewed all the Parlee and O'Reilly accounts from 2005 to 2009 and find that none were marked as “final” or “interim”; • whether adjustments were made to the accounts. There appears to be no such adjustments, except for some possible arithmetic errors; and • whether the client could only appreciate the value at the end of the retainer. This was not applicable, as on the basis of the agreement I find to exist between the parties, there were to be no adjustments at the end of the retainer, regardless of the value perceived to be obtained. b. — Natural Breaks 33 Parlee, relying on Re Romer, at paras. 293–94 and 301, Siegel, at paras. 8–9a and Abedi, at pp. 205–7, described the history of the concept of natural breaks, as an exception to the “end of cause or whole/entire contract” retainer and account situation: … Courts of Equity did not follow the traditional common law rules …, and applied a more flexible approach. These courts recognized that suits in equity, which would include suits for breach of trust such as that brought before the federal courts in the Litigation, could become complicated and lengthy, and might be divided into stages, or “phases” to use the terminology employed by the trial judge in this case. Accordingly, the Courts of Equity recognized that, in the course of such lengthy suits, a lawyer may properly send an account to his client from time to time, made out up to a certain date or a certain point that comprises a “natural break” in the progress of the litigation. This was an important feature of Chancery Practice. This important rule of equity prevailed after the 1873 union of the courts of common law and equity. 34 Thus, there was a time in equity that there were expected to be natural breaks in litigation and, as an exception to the common law principle of no account until the end of the litigation, it was changed to no account was to be delivered until that natural break occurred. 35 Originally a natural break was to trial, with an account following decision, and then a new retainer and account to the end of the succeeding appeal or appeals. As time went on, there were also agreed, or perceived, natural breaks leading to trial, such as close of pleadings, document production, questioning (as it is now called—then examination for discovery) and trial, as well as natural breaks after trial (leaves to appeal where required), and the appeal or appeals itself/themselves. … 38 […] it remains in the modern era that the facts of each case, not the common law, will determine whether the retainer ended with a natural break. c. — Continuous 39 Notwithstanding historical traditions, there were also continuous retainers—where one started to act for a party in a litigious cause and continued until the last appeal or until otherwise instructed (the latter usually on settlement or abandonment of further litigation). … 41 In this type of continuous litigation and continuous retainers, there are often several types of possible account scenarios to which counsel and the client may agree: (1) interim or provisional accounts (by definition, meaning pending the final account), or (2) periodic accounts (not conclusive, absent agreement as to whether or not they were interim or provisional, or final), or (3) final accounts (each starts on its own and stood on its own). In each of these cases, often the language used did/does not determine the facts, and therefore, when disputes arises/arose, such as here, the facts have/had to be determined. d. — Final = Stand Alone 42 The term “stand alone” is my own. Often in the parties' briefs, the word “final” was used to mean that it was at this point (and most often only at this point) that the rights to taxation arose. However, often in these contexts, the word “final” was not defined or clear. Did it mean that each account stood alone and was the subject of taxation, within any applicable limitation periods (statutorily or procedurally)? Or did it merely mean that the account would not change, and as such was “final” in a literal sense, but did not determine a right of taxation or establish a contracting out of the right to taxation (see the discussion in Robertson, at p 657–58 [WWR])? In my view, the term “stand alone” might be a better description to apply to an account which is itself subject to taxation on its own. It is a clearer term than “final” to mean that the rules of taxation/review apply to it alone. With this discussion, I treat “final” and “stand alone” accounts as synonymous. 3. — Types of Accounts and Taxation Consequences 44 Under the various types of retainers, accounts are most often periodic, which means that they are sent out at regular (mostly monthly here) or irregular intervals during the term of the retainer. However, there are no ipso facto taxation consequences. 45 Periodic accounts may be interim8 or final. An interim account is one that is not final, but is issued pending a final account, and may be changed directly at any future time or in the end result between the time it is issued and the final account. It is thus customary that interim accounts are not the subject of taxation individually, but rather only the final account. When the final account is taxed, all the interim accounts issued leading to the final account are taxable. 46 Final accounts are ones that conclude all truly interim or provisional accounts before them (in which case, as noted, all the interim accounts are part of that taxation), or are final and taxable in themselves, with no regard to other accounts. 47 While it may not have always been the case under common law imposed whole/entire contract retainers, I find that the law is clear that individual and periodic accounts can be final or stand alone, if consistent with the retainer applicable between the lawyer and client. … c. — Retainer 67 As noted, retainers can be: whole/entire contract, natural break, continuous, or stand alone. While there may be exceptions in specific cases by agreement, generally whole/entire contract final retainers and natural break retainers only have a final account at the end of the case, or at the end of the break. However, accounts under continuous retainers can be either provisional or final; and accounts under a stand-alone retainer are, by definition, final. Thus, to put it generally, it follows that if the Court finds each account final, the retainer is normally neither a whole/entire contract retainer nor a natural-breaks retainer. In this regard, the question of what was the retainer and whether the accounts are final, is a bit of a “chicken and egg” discussion. Thus, I need to determine which type of retainer can be eliminated from consideration and then look at the nature of the accounts. 68 Under the definition section of the New Rules, “retainer agreement” is defined as “An express or implied agreement between a lawyer and a client with respect to the payment by the client of the lawyer's charges …”. I note that this definition confirms the common law that a retainer agreement may be either express or implied. … In concluding that in the matter before him the retainer was not a “natural breaks retainer”, A.C.J. Rooke said, at paragraph 76: 76 Put another way, while the rationale of natural breaks for taxation purposes, as noted in Ladner, at p. 6, may have benefits for both client and lawyer, it is not, in the modern era, automatic, nor is it a matter of reasonableness. Rather, it depends on evidence of clear agreement. … In also concluding that the matter before him was not an “entire contract” retainer, his Lordship said, at paragraph 79: 79 Parlee, relying on: Sharma; Abedi; Fiset v. Falner, [2005] O.J. No. 4023, 142 ACWS (3d) 69 (SCJ.—Parell J), at paras. 40–41; and Re Fellowes, at para 8, and Davis), described modern litigation principles applicable to retainers and accounts in a way with which I agree: Modern Anglo-Canadian jurisprudence does not go nearly so far [as the old common law cases]…. Current legal principles recognize that there can be periodic accounts (final as to the work set out therein) if the agreement between the lawyer and the client permits such accounts. Such an agreement may be express or inferred. Indeed, where the evidence establishes that the retainer was to be based on hourly rates and time spent, and not on results achieved11, it will certainly be inferred that the account is periodic and final in relation to the work set out therein. The mere fact that some subsequent or last account might still be subject to taxation would not render subject to taxation any prior periodic or interim accounts (however they might be labelled) now otherwise out of time. [Emphasis added] In West v. Logie Family Law, 2018 ABCA 255, 2018 CarswellAlta 1411, 72 Alta. L.R. (6th) 52, 20 C.P.C. (8th) 223, the Court endorsed the factors set out in Samson Cree Nation v. O'Reilly & Associés, but went on to disagree that the test for granting an extension of time is a “low threshold”. The Court said: 19 As the chambers judge noted, this court endorsed the six factors to be considered for extending time in Samson Cree Nation v O'Reilly & Associés, 2014 ABCA 268 (Samson appeal) but the chambers judge went on to state that Chief Justice Wittmann in Attila (at para 35) indicated that the criteria “were not necessarily exhaustive and not complying with any one of them was not a precondition, but they were to be weighed together in context as a whole”. 20 However, despite initially stating the law correctly, the chambers judge went further to state at paragraph 25 that discretion to extend a time period should be exercised, “where there is some evidence that the account should be reviewed”, which he described as a “low threshold”. After stating at paragraph 26, “When a client seeks an explanation for their legal fees, and the [Alberta Rules of Court] provide for a process that does exactly that, this Court should not stand in the client's way except in the clearest of cases, for example where vexatious litigants advance baseless claims”. He then stated, “As long as there is some evidence that a client, in good faith, seeks an independent review of their legal fees, the fiat ought to be granted”. (See paragraph 10 above for the full quote of paragraphs 25 and 26 of the chambers judge's reasons.) 21 These are, quite simply, incorrect statements of the law. Nowhere in the case authorities of this court is there support for the chambers judge's view of the minimal requirement needed to permit an extension of the time for review of a lawyer's accounts. 22 Moreover, his statements do not reflect the policy behind the rule. The six month limit provided in rule 10.10, like the former rule 647, balances the client's right to review a legal account against the lawyer's right to have an account reviewed promptly: Samson appeal. Among other things, the limit seeks to make it easier to resolve disputes by avoiding the difficulty of assessing complaints about events years past, puts lawyers on notice that a client has concerns, encourages clients to voice their concerns close to the date they arise and allows lawyers to anticipate uncollectible receivables within a reasonable period of time: Twinn v Sawridge Band, 2012 ABQB 44 at para 38, 531 AR 158. The chambers judge's statements of the test to be applied ignore the need for balance between the client and lawyer by setting such a low threshold. His test sets a threshold so low it virtually eliminates the need to consider any criterion other than a client's bona fide intention to have legal fees reviewed. 23 The test stated by the chambers judge also failed to give effect to the time limitation in rule 10.10. As stated in Samson appeal at para 200: A litigant who misses a time limit is prima facie out of court. Time limits are not mere free advice; they are law. The dilatory party seeking relief does so on the grounds (inter alia) that barring it would be unjust. In Van Brabant v. Amonson, 2013 ABQB 547, 2013 CarswellAlta 1876, Justice Moen, in referring to Rule 10.10, said, at paragraphs 15, 17, and 18: 15 This rule has been interpreted by the courts to mean that the six-month limitation occurs after the final account has been rendered to the client: Samson Cree at para 120 and Sharma v. 643454 Alberta Ltd, 2006 ABQB 119 at para 139. … 17 Many cases have treated periodic accounts rendered by lawyers as being interim accounts. Each case was decided on its facts: Sharma at para 39. 18 A “final account is simply one that will not be changed”: Samson Cree at para 25. Moen, J. went on to say that a lawyer must inform his or her client of the limitation period within which the client may contest an account. The learned Chambers judge said, at paragraphs 39–42: 39 This section in the Retainer Letter entitled “Periodic Accounts” was therefore misleading to Ms. Amonson's clients. If each of the accounts were expected to be final, I would expect her to say so in this section of the Retainer Letter. I would expect lawyers to advise their clients of the limitation period in her Retainer Letter and also in each of the accounts that was sent out from time to time. The fact that Ms. Amonson did not warn her clients about the six-month limitation period in this section of her Retainer Letter suggests to me that she did not intend the six-month limitation period to apply. 40 I acknowledge that she urges her clients to bring any concerns to her immediately upon receipt. This does not, however, amount to a warning that if they do not to do so, a six-month limitation period would apply. 41 Lawyers have a duty to be forthright and honest with their clients. This includes warning their clients at the outset of their retainer of any limitation periods that apply including the limitation period with respect to complaints about accounts. If a lawyer did not warn clients about a limitation period on a file, that would be negligence. They should not be permitted to profit by not warning their clients about a limitation period for complaints about accounts. 42 Lawyers cannot expect clients to know about such limitation periods which are buried in the Rules of Court. Members of the public cannot be expected to know the ins and outs of those rules. Lawyers have a duty to warn their clients of this limitation period if they intend to rely on it. Justice Moen specifically disagreed with A.C.J. Rooke on the issue of “rupturing the solicitor-client relationship”, and said, at paragraphs 70–71: 70 It has been said in earlier cases that a client, who challenges a lawyer's account before a matter is concluded, is in danger of “rupturing the solicitor-client relationship.” The relationship between client and lawyer is one of trust. The lawyer holds knowledge that is mysterious to most lay people. Lay persons do not know the “cut and thrust” of the law and rely completely on their lawyers to succeed in a law suit. It is not difficult to understand where that common law principle arose. It must be very difficult for a client to challenge their lawyer's account when they are in the middle of litigation such as the Applicants are in this case. Therefore, a lay person could reasonably believe that a challenge to his lawyer on any matter, especially what the lawyer is charging, could damage or rupture their relationship. 71 I therefore respectfully disagree with Rooke ACJ in Samson Cree at para. 23 where he suggests that this common law concept should no longer apply. However, in West v. Logie Family Law, 2018 ABCA 255, 2018 CarswellAlta 1411, 72 Alta. L.R. (6th) 52, 20 C.P.C. (8th) 223, a three-member panel of the Court said, at paragraphs 33–35: 33 We note that we do not endorse the principle of “rupturing” the solicitor-client relationship as discussed in Van Brabant Estate (Re), 2013 ABQB 547 and which was relied upon by the chambers judge in para 24 of his decision. While it is usually not feasible for a client to discharge his counsel midway through a trial, the fact is that not only did the respondent not discharge the appellant following the conclusion of the trial in May 2015, he waited another 15 months before seeking to have the accounts taxed. Even if there is a principle of “rupturing” the solicitor-client relationship, it would have no applicability here given the facts of this case. 34 We note that counsel, particularly when acting for individuals, might consider advising their clients in writing that they have the right pursuant to the Rules of Court to review a retainer agreement and the lawyer's charges. This advice could be contained either in the retainer agreement itself or in a letter provided at the same time as the retainer agreement and acknowledged by the client. The precise wording of Rules 10.9 and 10.10 could be included and the client advised that an extension of time beyond that stipulated in Rule 10.10 is not easily obtained. 35 Counsel suggested that this may open the floodgates to reviewing lawyers' accounts. However, clients have the right to review a lawyer's account. Further, it may be preferable to have more reviews within the six months limitation, than to have reviews in some cases stretching back years. 5. Interim Accounts In Baxandall v. Peterson Hustwick Wetsch & Moffat (1994), 154 A.R. 353 (Q.B.), Madam Justice Nash heard an application by a client under then R 647 for an order permitting taxation of nine accounts rendered by her solicitors in respect of a domestic law file. Although the client's application was beyond the six-month limitation period for the first eight of the accounts, the court held that the taxing officer should be permitted to review them. At p. 357, her Ladyship said: In my opinion all the bills rendered prior to the rendering of the final bill were interim bills and for the purposes of taxation all the bills rendered should be considered as comprising part of the final bill. Furthermore, the rendering of interim accounts is an accepted practice. It is unrealistic to expect a client to subject each of these accounts to taxation where there is some dispute. It goes without saying that this would immediately result in a breakdown of the solicitor/client relationship. Therefore the applicant is entitled to have all the accounts taxed. Alternatively, if I am wrong in finding that each of the bills were mere statements of account showing the expenses to date, I am satisfied that the court has the jurisdiction to order that a paid bill be taxed even if the appointment to tax is filed outside six months. The applicant has the right to have the final bill taxed pursuant to rule 647. In my opinion the taxation officer cannot properly discharge his duty to tax an account unless he is also permitted to tax all of the previous account as all the accounts relate to essentially one matter. 6. Extension of Time It is clear from the rules and the case comments that the court will refuse to give leave to extend time for taxation by a client where inordinate delay has resulted in prejudice to the solicitor or it would be manifestly unjust to extend time. Oilexco Inc. v. MacKimmie Matthews (1997), 52 Alta. L.R. (3d) 412 (Master), at p. 420, per Master Laycock. In BA Capital Inc. v. Focused Money Solutions Inc., 2012 ABQB 379, 2012 CarswellAlta 1006 (Master), the applicants sought leave “to have the accounts of their solicitors … reviewed after the passage of the 6 month period has passed.” In refusing to grant leave, Master Laycock said, at paragraphs 8–10, and 12–14, the learned Master said: 8 In this application the first consideration is whether or not the applicants can satisfy me that they have a reasonable excuse for failing to bring the disputed accounts before a Review Officer within six months of the bill being delivered. In the case of a series of interim accounts, it is the date of the delivery of the final bill that is material. See Baxandall v. Peterson Hustwick Wetsch & Moffat (1994), 154 A.R. 353 (Q.B.). 9 In this case the applicant has provided no evidence in his affidavit to explain the 16 month delay following the final account in bringing this application or when he became concerned about the size of the account or the performance of the law firm. An explanation for his concern about the size of the account and the performance of the law firm was given during argument, but that is not evidence. 10 If a reasonable explanation is provided to the court to explain the delay in bringing the accounts to a Review Officer, then the court must consider whether or not there's any evidence of prejudice to the law firm in bringing the matter forward. While there is no evidence of prejudice, the question of prejudice never arises in this matter because there is no explanation given for the delay in bringing the accounts before the Review Officer. … 12 At a minimum, the evidence that an applicant must bring is why there was a delay in bringing the issue to a Review Officer. In many of the applications that we hear, the clients affidavit expresses a lack of knowledge of the process. They have paid the account and have no knowledge that the account can be reviewed. If the file is incomplete when the solicitor-client relationship terminates, it is often the clients second law firm that advises the client of the right to have the account reviewed. 13 In Oilexco Inc. v. MacKimmie Matthews 1997 CarswellAlta 415, 203 A.R. 213, 12 C.P.C. (4th) 352, 52 L.R. (3rd) 412 a third party who, pursuant to an agreement, was liable for the payment of another's legal account did not obtain copies of accounts until after the time for their review had passed. Their explanation for the delay in bringing the application before the then Taxation Officer (now Review Officer) was accepted. Given the circumstances it was determined that there was no inordinate delay in bringing the matter forward. There was no evidence of prejudice to the law firm and the matter was allowed to proceed to taxation. 14 Since there is no adequate evidence explaining the delay, the application for leave to have the accounts reviewed is dismissed. In Attila Dogan Construction and Installation Co. Inc. v. Bennett Jones LLP, 2015 ABQB 407, 2015 CarswellAlta 3128, Chief Justice Wittmann said: 33 The factors guiding the discretion of a Court in extending the time, within the limitation period are delay, prejudice, first intent to tax (assess the accounts), evidence of overcharging, agreement as to amount and the relationship between lawyer and client. 34 The above factors as relevant criteria were set out in detail in Samson Cree First Nation (QB) at paras. 168–232. 35 In Samson Cree First Nation (CA), the Court of Appeal agreed with the list of relevant criteria and also indicated they were not necessarily exhaustive and not complying with any one of them was not a precondition, but they were to be weighed together in context as a whole. In West v. Logie Family Law, 2018 ABCA 255, 2018 CarswellAlta 1411, 72 Alta. L.R. (6th) 52, 20 C.P.C. (8th) 223, the Court said that applications for an extension of time under Rule 10.10(2) should not be made ex parte. The Court said, at paragraph 36: 36 We also question whether it is appropriate to extend the deadline in Rule 10.10(2) by way of an ex parte fiat. Masters should direct a party seeking an ex parte fiat in such circumstances to give notice to the opposing lawyer/law firm or client, to provide an evidentiary basis for the requested extension and consider whether an order rather than a fiat should be granted if the test is met.
